neighborhoods_visited: Historic District - Trust Squares and Factor's Walk
guide_description: Three days covering Savannah's essential layers: the colonial grid of live-oak squares and riverfront warehouses, the ornate Victorian residential district anchored by Forsyth Park, and the atmospheric marshland edge where the city gives way to tidal creeks and one of America's most celebrated cemeteries. Each day is geographically self-contained.

days.cluster_tagline: Oglethorpe's colonial grid - trust squares, cotton commerce, and the cobblestone riverfront
days.neighborhood_focus: Historic District - Trust Squares and Factor's Walk
days.neighborhood_description: The northern half of Savannah's National Historic Landmark District, where James Oglethorpe's 1733 town plan survives almost intact. Twenty-two original squares shaded by live oaks draped in Spanish moss alternate with Federal and Regency townhouses. The bluff drops steeply to the Savannah River, where Factor's Walk - a network of iron-bridged cotton warehouses built into the hillside - marks the commercial heart of the antebellum South.

morning.notes: The central trust square of Oglethorpe's original plan, dominated by a bronze statue of the general himself. Early morning - before 9am - is when the Spanish moss catches low-angled light and the square is empty of tour groups. The bench from the Forrest Gump bus stop scenes was placed here during filming but has since been moved to the Savannah History Museum; do not expect to find it.

walk_to_next.to: Cathedral Basilica of Saint John the Baptist

afternoon.activity_title: Cathedral Basilica of Saint John the Baptist
afternoon.notes: The largest Catholic church in Georgia, rebuilt after an 1898 fire in French Gothic style with twin spires visible across the Lafayette Square treetops. The interior has 19 hand-painted murals and a restored pipe organ. Enter from the Lafayette Square side rather than the main door on Harris Street - the approach through the square frames both spires cleanly.

evening.notes: The network of iron bridges and ramps connecting the bluff-level counting houses to the lower river wharves, built in the 1820s when Savannah was the world's largest cotton market. Walk the upper iron-bridge level first for the structural and logistical logic to make sense, then descend to River Street for the direct water view. Sunset over the Savannah River from the lower level, with container ships from the Port of Savannah still passing, is one of the city's genuinely cinematic moments.

if_time_permits.activity_title: Telfair Academy of Arts and Sciences
if_time_permits.notes: The oldest public art museum in the American Southeast, housed in William Jay's 1819 Regency mansion on Telfair Square. The Octagon Room at the building's core is the architectural centerpiece - Jay's interpretation of a Soane-influenced top-lit rotunda. Good rainy-day option that most visitors skip in favor of the squares.

The largest of Savannah's squares and the first laid out by Oglethorpe in 1733, positioned along the main Bull Street corridor between the river bluff and the trust lots. The central obelisk marks the grave of Nathanael Greene, Revolutionary War general. The surrounding Christ Church building dates to 1838 and was the site of Georgia's first Sunday school.

days.cluster_name: Forsyth Park and the Victorian District
days.cluster_tagline: Antebellum mansions, the city's grandest fountain, and the ornate residential streets south of the trust lots
days.neighborhood_description: The southern extension of Savannah's historic grid, anchored by the 30-acre Forsyth Park and framed by Italianate and Queen Anne houses built during the city's post-Civil War cotton revival. The Victorian District, immediately south of Gaston Street, preserves the densest concentration of late 19th-century architecture in Georgia.

morning.notes: John Norris's 1868 Italianate mansion on Monterey Square, made famous by John Berendt's Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil. The guided tour covers the ground floor and carriage house - the second floor remains a private residence. Book the first morning tour slot (usually 10:30am) to avoid the midday bunching of groups. The ironwork on the facade is among the finest cast iron in the South.

afternoon.notes: Savannah's central park, laid out in 1851 in the style of a French formal garden. The white cast-iron fountain at the north end - modeled on a design exhibited at the 1858 Paris Exhibition - is the most photographed object in the city. Walk the full perimeter: the Confederate memorial at the south end is rarely visited but the surrounding Beaux-Arts landscaping and the view back north to the fountain from that distance is far better than the standard close-up shot.

evening.notes: The streets immediately south of Forsyth Park - particularly Gwinnett, Bolton, and Anderson streets between Whitaker and Habersham - hold the highest concentration of intact Queen Anne, Folk Victorian, and shotgun houses in Savannah. Walk south on Whitaker and return north on Habersham to cover both sides of the street lighting. Porches here face west and catch amber late-afternoon light that the live-oak canopy filters into something worth lingering for.

if_time_permits.notes: William Jay's 1819 Regency masterpiece on Oglethorpe Square - the most architecturally sophisticated antebellum house in Savannah. The restored urban slave quarters behind the main house are among the most complete surviving examples in the United States and are the interpretive focus of the current tour. Telfair Museums ticket covers this site and the Academy.

days.cluster_tagline: Live oaks over tidal marsh - the city's most atmospheric cemetery and the working waterfront at Thunderbolt
days.neighborhood_description: The eastern edge of Savannah, where the urban grid dissolves into tidal creeks, bluff ridges, and maritime forest. Bonaventure Cemetery occupies a bluff above the Wilmington River, its avenues of live oaks and 19th-century monuments forming one of the most celebrated burial landscapes in the American South. The adjacent fishing village of Thunderbolt preserves a working waterfront that has changed little since the shrimp-boat era.

morning.notes: Established on the grounds of a colonial plantation, Bonaventure occupies a river bluff under a continuous canopy of live oaks so dense the moss-hung branches arch over the avenues like cathedral vaulting. Arrive before 10am when the eastern light comes through horizontally and the tour buses have not yet arrived. The section containing Johnny Mercer's grave is in the far northeastern corner near the river - worth the walk for the view down the Wilmington River bluff from that end. The Bird Girl statue made famous by Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil has been moved to the Telfair's Jepson Center.

afternoon.notes: A working shrimp-boat and sport-fishing village on the Wilmington River just south of Bonaventure, almost entirely overlooked by visitors. The marina on River Drive still has active shrimp trawlers - the docks are publicly accessible and the boats come in late morning. The row of small restaurants on the bluff above the marina serves some of the most credibly local boiled shrimp and fried fish in the Savannah area, sourced directly from boats below.

evening.notes: Noble Jones's 1736 tabby-construction colonial estate on the Isle of Hope, accessed via a 1.5-mile oak-canopied entry avenue that is one of the most photographed natural corridors in the American South. The avenue runs due east-west - afternoon light comes straight down the tunnel of trees from behind the visitor as you walk toward the ruins. The tabby fortification ruins at the end of the avenue are the oldest surviving colonial structure in Georgia. State park entry fee applies.

if_time_permits.notes: A small community museum in the former A.S. Varn oyster and crab factory on Moon River, preserving the history of the Gullah Geechee community that worked the coastal fisheries here from Reconstruction into the 1980s. Justice Clarence Thomas grew up in this community. The building sits on a tidal creek with the original processing equipment intact - rarely crowded and genuinely affecting.
